steps.d: “Check tomorrow’s weather in Hangzhou and add an umbrella reminder.” This is just a piece of text; from here on it’s a relay through the layers below.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: Natural language is the most universal “interface”: you don’t need to learn any commands; the system turns your words into actions.

steps.t: The agent app takes the job
steps.d: The app wraps your words in a “system prompt” (identity, rules, list of available tools), and the safety layer first checks the request itself.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: The model can only write text; deterministic work like taking the job, assembling context and safety checks goes to ordinary programs, which are more reliable and easier to audit.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.d: Memory / RAG retrieves your preferences (example: time zone = Shanghai, reminders default to 8 a.m.) and puts them into the context.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: The model’s parameters don’t change in use; new information can only be seen by it if it’s “put into the context”.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.t: Sent to inference serving, tokenized first
steps.d: The whole text goes to the inference service and is batched with other people’s requests. The tokenizer first cuts the text into tokens.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: The model can only process numbers; subword splitting strikes a balance between “vocabulary size” and “sequence length”.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.t: First, the parts: neurons and the training loop
steps.d: Every part of an LLM is built from “weighted sum + activation” neurons; the parameters are their weights and biases, learned by the loop “forward → loss → backprop → update”.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: Simple parts can be computed in parallel in bulk and differentiated everywhere, which is what lets gradient descent tune billions of parameters automatically.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.t: The model computes layer by layer
steps.d: Tokens become vectors and are processed by dozens of Transformer blocks: attention exchanges information and the FFN digests individually. Each layer’s K and V are stored in the KV cache.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: Each layer does only a little processing; stacked layer upon layer they get from “literal” to “meaning”; residuals and normalization make dozens of layers trainable.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.t: Writes a decision: check the weather first
steps.d: The output scoring layer scores every candidate token, softmax turns scores into probabilities, and then one is sampled. Token by token it writes “call get_weather first”.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: Outputting probabilities rather than a single answer can express “uncertainty”, and in training they can be used directly to compute the loss.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.d: The model writes {"name":"get_weather","arguments":{"city":"Hangzhou","date":"tomorrow"}}. It’s the app that actually checks the weather.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: The JSON format is fixed, so the program can reliably parse and validate it; mistakes can be detected and rejected.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.t: Run it and feed back the result
steps.d: The app calls the weather API, gets “light rain, 80% chance of precipitation” (sample data), appends the result to the context as text, and starts the next loop.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: The model has no other senses: a tool result only becomes “visible” to it in the next loop once it’s written into the context.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.d: Earlier content is already in the KV cache, so only the new tool result needs computing. The model decides: it will rain → a reminder is needed.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: Earlier K and V don’t change, so storing them avoids recomputing the whole text for every new word — trading memory for time.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.d: Creating a reminder is a “write action”. Under the permission rules, either you authorized it beforehand or a confirmation card asks for your OK.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: Write actions have real consequences and are hard to undo; human confirmation catches model misjudgements and prompt injection.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.d: Calls create_reminder(tomorrow 8:00 a.m., “bring an umbrella”); it returns success and the result is fed back.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: It’s the same “think → act → observe” loop: one process handles tasks with any number of steps.
steps.f: Parts in this step (tap for the full card):

steps.d: The model decides the task is done and streams the answer to you word by word: “Light rain in Hangzhou tomorrow; I’ve added an umbrella reminder for 8:00 tomorrow morning.”
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: The model writes token by token anyway; showing it as it writes saves you from waiting.

steps.t: Behind the scenes: where these skills come from
steps.d: None of it is learned on the spot: pretraining gave language and common sense, supervised fine-tuning taught tool calls in the right format, preference alignment made answers appropriate, and RL made multi-step tasks more reliable.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: Training in stages: the stage with the most data learns general abilities, the stages with less but refined data learn formats and behaviour — each plays to its strengths.

steps.d: This time it’s all text. If you sent speech or a screenshot, it would first go through the audio or vision encoder and become vectors before entering the LLM.
steps.w: 🧠 Why it’s designed this way: Once images and sound are turned into vector sequences, the rest of the computation fully reuses the same LLM.
